8	Do they originate in the vision encoder's pretrained features, emerge through LLM processing, or arise from task-specific fine-tuning?
9

11	Grant et al.~\cite{grant2026} showed that the visual pathway dominates action generation across multiple VLA architectures, with ablations to the language stream producing minimal behavioral degradation.
12	Independently, Hou et al.~\cite{hou2026} and Fei et al.~\cite{fei2025} demonstrated that VLAs largely ignore language instructions during policy execution.
13	These findings challenge the prevailing narrative but remain at the behavioral level---they reveal \emph{what} drives VLA outputs without explaining \emph{where} action-relevant structure resides in the representation space.
14	No prior work has performed a representational decomposition that measures each component's independent contribution to action-relevant structure.
15	Without this, we cannot determine whether fine-tuning truly injects action knowledge or merely learns to route pre-existing structure.
16	
17	We present the first systematic representational and functional analysis of a VLA.
18	Taking OpenVLA-7B~\cite{kim2024_openvla} as a case study, we decompose its processing pipeline into constituent components: the frozen SigLIP vision encoder~\cite{zhai2023_siglip} with MLP projector, every layer of the Llama-2 7B backbone, and the readout token position.
19	We apply Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} to measure geometric alignment with the action space and train functional probes to measure action decodability.
20	A $2 \times 2$ factorial design crossing training status (trained vs.\ untrained LLM) with instruction presence (with vs.\ without) isolates each factor's contribution.
21	External baselines---DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2} (vision-only) and CLIP ViT-L/14~\cite{radford2021_clip} (vision-language pretrained, no VLA training)---anchor our comparisons.
22	
23	Three findings emerge from experiments on the LIBERO-Goal benchmark~\cite{liu2023_libero}.
24	\textbf{First}, frozen vision-language encoders provide the dominant action-relevant geometric structure.
25	SigLIP+Projector achieves the highest action-space alignment (RSA $\rho = 0.615$), followed by CLIP ($\rho = 0.557$), both far exceeding the vision-only DINOv2 ($\rho = 0.388$).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) achieve impressive robotic manipulation performance by fine-tuning large language models on robot demonstration data~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}.
The dominant architecture grafts a frozen vision encoder onto a pretrained LLM backbone, then fine-tunes the system end-to-end to map visual observations and language instructions to continuous actions~\cite{karamcheti2024}.
An implicit assumption underlies this paradigm: fine-tuning injects action-relevant representational knowledge into the LLM.
But where do action representations actually come from?
Do they originate in the vision encoder's pretrained features, emerge through LLM processing, or arise from task-specific fine-tuning?

Recent work reveals cracks in this assumption.
Grant et al.~\cite{grant2026} showed that the visual pathway dominates action generation across multiple VLA architectures, with ablations to the language stream producing minimal behavioral degradation.
Independently, Hou et al.~\cite{hou2026} and Fei et al.~\cite{fei2025} demonstrated that VLAs largely ignore language instructions during policy execution.
These findings challenge the prevailing narrative but remain at the behavioral level---they reveal \emph{what} drives VLA outputs without explaining \emph{where} action-relevant structure resides in the representation space.
No prior work has performed a representational decomposition that measures each component's independent contribution to action-relevant structure.
Without this, we cannot determine whether fine-tuning truly injects action knowledge or merely learns to route pre-existing structure.

We present the first systematic representational and functional analysis of a VLA.
Taking OpenVLA-7B~\cite{kim2024_openvla} as a case study, we decompose its processing pipeline into constituent components: the frozen SigLIP vision encoder~\cite{zhai2023_siglip} with MLP projector, every layer of the Llama-2 7B backbone, and the readout token position.
We apply Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} to measure geometric alignment with the action space and train functional probes to measure action decodability.
A $2 \times 2$ factorial design crossing training status (trained vs.\ untrained LLM) with instruction presence (with vs.\ without) isolates each factor's contribution.
External baselines---DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2} (vision-only) and CLIP ViT-L/14~\cite{radford2021_clip} (vision-language pretrained, no VLA training)---anchor our comparisons.

Three findings emerge from experiments on the LIBERO-Goal benchmark~\cite{liu2023_libero}.
\textbf{First}, frozen vision-language encoders provide the dominant action-relevant geometric structure.
SigLIP+Projector achieves the highest action-space alignment (RSA $\rho = 0.615$), followed by CLIP ($\rho = 0.557$), both far exceeding the vision-only DINOv2 ($\rho = 0.388$).
Yet DINOv2 matches SigLIP+Projector in action prediction capacity ($R^2 = 0.712$ vs.\ $0.706$, $p = 0.22$), revealing a geometric-functional dissociation: VL pretraining provides geometric alignment with the action space without increasing raw decodability.
\textbf{Second}, the LLM degrades distributed geometric alignment (RSA $0.615 \to 0.501$) but concentrates a functionally superior signal at the readout token ($R^2 = 0.731$, exceeding the projector's $0.706$).
This concentration is training-dependent: an untrained LLM's readout achieves only $R^2 = 0.686$, falling below the projector baseline.
\textbf{Third}, training teaches routing, not creating.
Distributed RSA is training-invariant ($\Delta = 0.021$, 95\% CI includes zero, $p = 0.20$), while readout concentration shows a large training effect ($\Delta = 0.045$, $p < 0.0001$).
Language instructions affect neither metric.

These results reframe how we understand VLA representations and carry direct design implications: vision encoder pretraining quality---not LLM fine-tuning---is the primary lever for action-relevant structure~\cite{haon2025}.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item The first systematic representational decomposition of a VLA, quantifying each component's contribution to action-relevant structure with both geometric (RSA) and functional (probe $R^2$) metrics.
    \item Discovery of a geometric-functional dissociation: vision-language pretraining provides geometric alignment with the action space beyond what raw information content predicts, while vision-only features are functionally rich but geometrically dissimilar.
    \item Evidence that LLM fine-tuning teaches information routing---concentrating pre-existing vision-encoder structure at the readout position---rather than creating new action-relevant representations.
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	We investigate where action-relevant representations originate within a vision-language-action (VLA) model by combining representational similarity analysis, functional probing, and kernel alignment across a factorial design of training and instruction conditions.
5	
6	\subsection{Model and Data}
7	\label{sec:model_data}
8	
9	\paragraph{Architecture.}
10	We study OpenVLA-7B~\cite{kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024}, a VLA model comprising four components: (1)~a SigLIP-SO400M vision encoder~\cite{zhai2023_siglip} that maps RGB observations to patch-level visual tokens, (2)~an MLP projector that maps vision tokens into the language model's embedding space, (3)~a Llama-2 7B language backbone (32 transformer layers) that processes the concatenated sequence of projected image tokens and tokenized language instructions, and (4)~an action head that decodes 7-dimensional continuous actions (3D translation, 3D rotation, 1D gripper) from the final hidden states.
11	
12	\paragraph{Training data.}
13	We fine-tune OpenVLA on the LIBERO-10 split~\cite{liu2023_libero}, which contains 10 tabletop manipulation tasks with 50 human demonstrations each (500 demonstrations total).
14	We evaluate generalization on LIBERO-Goal, an out-of-distribution benchmark where episodes share initial object configurations but differ in goal specifications.
15	
16	\paragraph{Untrained control.}
17	To isolate the LLM's learned contribution from the vision encoder's pretrained geometry, we construct an untrained control by calling \texttt{from\_config()} to reinitialize all LLM parameters (6.74B weights drawn from random initialization) while preserving the frozen SigLIP encoder (0.80B pretrained weights).
18	The untrained model processes identical visual inputs through an identical vision encoder but lacks any learned language or action structure in its LLM layers.
19	
20	\subsection{Representation Extraction}
21	\label{sec:rep_extraction}
22	
23	We extract representations from five sources spanning the VLA processing pipeline and two external baselines:
24	
25	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),nosep,leftmargin=*]
26	    \item \textbf{SigLIP+Projector} --- the vision encoder output after MLP projection into the LLM's input space, before any LLM processing. This captures the representation that the LLM receives as input.
27	    \item \textbf{LLM image\_mean} --- the mean activation across all image token positions at each of the 32 LLM layers. This captures how the LLM transforms distributed visual information through its depth.
28	    \item \textbf{LLM last\_preaction} --- the activation at the final token position before action decoding (the readout token) at each LLM layer. This captures the representation from which actions are directly decoded.
29	    \item \textbf{DINOv2 ViT-L/14}~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2} \texttt{cls\_token} --- a vision-only baseline pretrained with self-supervised objectives and no language supervision.
30	    \item \textbf{CLIP ViT-L/14}~\cite{radford2021_clip} \texttt{patch\_mean} --- a vision-language baseline pretrained on image-text pairs, serving as a generalization control for VL pretraining effects independent of the VLA pipeline.
31	\end{enumerate}
32	
33	Sources (a)--(c) probe representations within the VLA model itself, while (d) and (e) provide external references with no VLA training signal.
34	
35	\paragraph{Factorial design.}
36	We cross two factors in a $2 \times 2$ design: \emph{training status} (trained vs.\ untrained LLM) and \emph{instruction presence} (with vs.\ without language instruction).
37	This yields four conditions per LLM representation source, enabling us to disentangle the contributions of LLM training and language grounding to action-relevant structure.
38	External baselines (d) and (e) are evaluated once, as they are independent of both factors.
39	
40	\subsection{Representational Similarity Analysis}
41	\label{sec:rsa}
42	
43	We adopt Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008} to quantify the geometric alignment between neural representations and the action space.
44	
45	\paragraph{Representational dissimilarity matrices.}
46	For a set of $n$ observations, we compute an $n \times n$ representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM) for each representation source using Euclidean distance between representation vectors.
47	We similarly construct an action RDM from the 7-dimensional action vectors.
48	
49	\paragraph{RSA correlation.}
50	We measure alignment between a representation RDM and the action RDM via Spearman rank correlation $\rho$ between their upper-triangular elements.
51	Higher $\rho$ indicates that observations with similar representations also have similar actions, i.e., the representation geometry mirrors the action space geometry.
52	
53	\paragraph{Statistical inference.}
54	We compute 95\% confidence intervals from 10{,}000 bootstrap resamples of observation pairs for all pairwise comparisons.
55	RSA is computed per task and aggregated across the 10 tasks.
56	
57	\subsection{Functional Action Probes}
58	\label{sec:probes}
59	
60	RSA measures geometric alignment but does not assess whether action information is linearly decodable from representations.
61	We complement RSA with functional probing~\cite{alain2017} to measure the action information accessible to a lightweight decoder.
62	
63	\paragraph{Probe architecture.}
64	We train two-layer MLP probes (Linear $\to$ ReLU $\to$ Linear) mapping from the representation dimensionality to a 256-dimensional hidden layer and then to the 7-dimensional action space.
65	
66	\paragraph{Training protocol.}
67	Probes are optimized with Adam (learning rate $10^{-3}$, batch size 256) for 50 epochs with early stopping (patience 5 epochs on validation loss).
68	Representations are frozen throughout; only probe parameters are updated.
69	We use per-task 80/20 train/validation splits and report mean $R^2$ across the 7 action dimensions as the primary metric.
70	
71	\paragraph{Action-delta probes.}
72	In addition to predicting absolute actions $\mathbf{a}_t$, we train probes to predict action deltas $\Delta\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{a}_{t+1} - \mathbf{a}_t$, which capture the dynamic component of action structure independent of the current action magnitude.
73	
74	\paragraph{Statistical comparison.}
75	We use bootstrap paired comparison (10{,}000 resamples) to test whether $R^2$ differences between representation sources are statistically significant.
76	
77	\subsection{Centered Kernel Alignment}
78	\label{sec:cka}
79	
80	RSA captures local geometric alignment---whether pairwise distances in representation space mirror those in action space.
81	To assess global structural preservation, we additionally employ Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)~\cite{kornblith2019} in two variants.
82	
83	\paragraph{Linear CKA.}
84	Linear CKA computes the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion between linear kernel matrices of two representation sets.
85	It is invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic scaling, making it sensitive to global structure rather than local distance preservation.
86	
87	\paragraph{RDM kernel CKA.}
88	We also compute CKA using the RDMs themselves as kernel matrices, providing a bridge between the local sensitivity of RSA and the global perspective of linear CKA.
89	
90	\paragraph{Dimensionality caveat.}
91	When comparing high-dimensional representations (e.g., 4096-D LLM activations) with low-dimensional action vectors (7-D), linear CKA may be dominated by the few directions that span the action space, potentially inflating similarity estimates.
92	We report both CKA variants alongside RSA to ensure that conclusions are robust to metric choice.
93

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\subsection{Vision-Language-Action Models}

VLAs repurpose pretrained vision-language models as robotic policies by fine-tuning them on demonstration data.
RT-2~\cite{brohan2023_rt2} established the paradigm by showing that a large vision-language model can be directly fine-tuned to output robotic actions tokenized as text, transferring web-scale knowledge to manipulation tasks.
OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla} made this architecture open-source, building on the Prismatic VLM framework~\cite{karamcheti2024} with a frozen SigLIP encoder~\cite{zhai2023_siglip} and a Llama-2 backbone.
$\pi_0$~\cite{black2024_pi0} departed from autoregressive action decoding in favor of flow matching, while retaining the frozen-encoder-plus-LLM structure.
A common architectural choice across these models is to freeze the vision encoder and fine-tune only the LLM and projector, embedding an implicit assumption: fine-tuning injects action-relevant knowledge into the LLM.
Our work tests this assumption directly at the representational level and finds that it does not hold---action-relevant geometric structure originates in the vision encoder and is routed, not created, by fine-tuning.

\subsection{Understanding VLA Representations}

A growing body of work investigates how VLAs process information internally.
Haon et al.~\cite{haon2025} performed the first mechanistic interpretability study of VLAs, identifying causally relevant attention heads and demonstrating activation steering for behavior modification.
Grant et al.~\cite{grant2026} showed across six VLA architectures that the visual pathway dominates action generation, with language stream ablations causing minimal behavioral degradation---a behavioral-level finding consistent with our representational-level observation of vision encoder dominance.
Swann et al.~\cite{swann2026} applied sparse autoencoders to OpenVLA, discovering interpretable monosemantic features at the individual-neuron level.
Rizzardo et al.~\cite{rizzardo2026} characterized VLA representations through the lens of observability and controllability, measuring how well internal features predict and steer downstream behavior.
Molinari et al.~\cite{molinari2025} probed OpenVLA for world-model properties, finding that the model encodes spatial and physical state information in its intermediate representations.

These studies illuminate different facets of VLA internals but leave a gap that our work addresses.
Grant et al.\ operate at the behavioral level (input ablations and output measurements) without examining representation geometry.
Swann et al.\ and Molinari et al.\ analyze individual features or semantic properties without quantifying how much action-relevant structure each architectural component contributes.
Haon et al.\ identify causal mechanisms but do not decompose where the underlying representations originate.
No prior work compares trained and untrained models to isolate training's contribution, and none reports the geometric-functional dissociation we observe between vision-language and vision-only encoders.

\subsection{Representational Analysis Methods}

Our methodology draws on a toolkit developed across neuroscience and deep learning.
Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, originally designed to compare neural recordings with computational models, quantifies geometric alignment between representation spaces via pairwise dissimilarity correlations.
Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)~\cite{kornblith2019} provides a complementary global measure invariant to orthogonal transformations, enabling comparison of representations across architectures and dimensionalities.
Linear probing~\cite{alain2017} assesses the functional content of representations by training lightweight decoders on frozen activations; Belinkov~\cite{belinkov2022} surveys its extensive use in NLP for analyzing linguistic structure at each layer of pretrained models.

These tools have been widely applied to vision models and language models in isolation, but their joint application to VLA pipelines---where vision, language, and action spaces intersect---is largely unexplored.
We combine RSA, CKA, and probing in a factorial design to provide the first systematic representational decomposition of a VLA, measuring both geometric alignment and functional decodability across all architectural components and training conditions.
The multi-metric approach proves essential: we show that linear CKA and RSA can produce divergent rankings of the same representations (Section~\ref{sec:vision_dominance}), underscoring the need for methodological plurality in representation analysis.

\subsection{Vision-Language Pretraining}

The vision encoders in modern VLAs inherit their representations from large-scale pretraining.
CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip} and SigLIP~\cite{zhai2023_siglip} learn visual features aligned to language through contrastive objectives on image-text pairs, while DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2} learns from self-supervised vision objectives without language supervision.
Prior work has shown that these pretraining paradigms produce qualitatively different representation geometries, but their downstream consequences for action-relevant structure in VLAs have not been characterized.
Our finding of a geometric-functional dissociation---VL-pretrained encoders achieve substantially higher geometric alignment with the action space than DINOv2 yet comparable functional decodability---provides the first direct evidence that language-grounded pretraining shapes the geometry, but not the information content, of action-relevant visual representations.
